title: How Chatbots Work
objective: After this level you can explain in simple terms how language models predict text.
summary: A chatbot runs on a large language model that writes by predicting a likely next token, again and again. Trained on huge amounts of text, it sounds fluent but can be confidently wrong.

cards.headline: Your phone's keyboard already plays a chatbot's favorite game.
cards.body: Type "see you" and it suggests "soon." Britannica describes large language models, the engines inside chatbots, as advanced versions of that same predictive text: they aim to produce the most probable words for your prompt. So how does a guessing game write whole paragraphs, and why is it sometimes wrong?

cards.headline: One token at a time
cards.body: A language model reads and writes in tokens: small chunks of text, usually a few characters long. Given your question, it works out which token is likely to come next, adds it, and asks the same question again with the longer text. A poem, a recipe or a history essay is built this way, one small prediction after another. There's no script hidden inside. There's only "what comes next?", asked over and over.

cards.headline: Trained on mountains of text
cards.body: Where do the predictions come from? Level 91's machine learning. In training, a model works through huge amounts of text, trillions of tokens, practicing predicting what comes next. The first large language models followed a design called the transformer, introduced in 2017. Chatbots add a finishing step: when OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in November 2022, it described fine-tuning the model with human feedback so it would answer in a conversational way.

cards.fact: Fluent is not the same as true.
cards.context: A model predicts the most probable words; making text sound right is not the same as checking it. So it can present something false in the same confident tone as something true, which is called a hallucination. In June 2023, a US federal judge fined two lawyers and their firm $5,000 for a brief citing six court cases that didn't exist. ChatGPT had made them up.

mascot.line: Sounding sure and being right are two different skills. Check the second one yourself.

cards.headline: Chatbots: decoded
learned: Language models write one predicted token at a time
They are trained on huge amounts of text
Chatbots are further tuned with human feedback (2022)
They can be confidently wrong: hallucinations

questions.prompt: While a language model writes a reply, what does it do at each step?

options.label: It looks up the next line in a fixed script
It checks each sentence against a fact database
options.rationale: Its core job is prediction, not fact-checking.

options.label: It predicts a likely next token and adds it
It copies a stored answer to the whole question
options.rationale: It builds the reply one token at a time.

questions.explanation: A language model writes by predicting a likely next token, adding it to the text and repeating.

questions.prompt: Why can a chatbot state something false in a confident tone?

options.label: It predicts likely-sounding text instead of checking it
It is programmed to be wrong some of the time
options.rationale: Nothing tells it to be wrong; it predicts probable text.

options.label: It runs out of tokens halfway through
It only ever learned from fake documents
options.rationale: It learned from huge amounts of ordinary text.

questions.explanation: A model produces the most probable words; sounding right is not the same as being checked, so it can hallucinate confidently.

questions.prompt: Level 91's spam filter learned from labeled emails. What does a language model learn from in training?

options.label: Emails labeled spam or not spam
options.rationale: That's the spam filter's training data.

options.label: Chess positions searched at high speed
Rules typed in by programmers one by one
options.rationale: Machine learning finds patterns instead of being handed rules.

options.label: Huge amounts of text, by predicting what comes next

questions.explanation: Language models are trained on trillions of tokens of text by practicing predicting the next token.
